html:
Surah An-Nās (Mankind) is the 114th and final surah of the Qur’an — six short verses, Makkī by the dominant classification of Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, with a minority Madanī opinion rooted in the surah’s linked occasion of revelation with Surah al-Falaq. It is one of the Muʿawwidhatān — the “Two Refuges” — the pair with which Allah closed the Qur’an and which the Prophet ﷺ took as his nightly protection and his after-prayer practice. Where Al-Falaq teaches refuge from external harms — darkness, envy, sorcery — An-Nās teaches refuge from the internal intrusion: the whisper that bypasses the eyes and ears and lands directly in the chest. Ibn Kathīr frames the whole surah as a single defensive formula: Allah’s servant is told to invoke his Lord with three titles — Rabb (Lord/Nurturer), Malik (King/Sovereign), Ilāh (God worthy of worship) — before naming the enemy against whom refuge is sought. The three-title opening is itself the content: no refuge is adequate unless the one giving refuge is simultaneously the one who created you, owns you, and deserves your worship. Classical mufassirūn note the ascending order — lordship (rubūbiyyah) is universal, sovereignty is particular to His kingdom, and divinity (ulūhiyyah) is the highest claim because it names the exclusive right to be worshipped.

The authentic practice of the Prophet ﷺ with the Muʿawwidhatān is firmly established across the Ṣaḥīḥayn and the Sunan. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5017 records ʿĀ’ishah’s narration: “When the Prophet ﷺ went to bed every night, he would cup his hands together and blow into them, then recite in them Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad, Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-falaq, and Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-nās, then he would wipe with them whatever he could of his body — starting with his head and face and the front of his body — doing this three times.” This is the sunnah of the three Quls (Ikhlāṣ, Falaq, Nās), and it establishes An-Nās as a nightly protection, not an occasional recitation. Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2903 (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ) and Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1523 both record ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir: the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to recite the Muʿawwidhāt after every obligatory prayer. Al-Albānī graded the after-prayer narration ṣaḥīḥ in Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan Abī Dāwūd. Sunan al-Nasā’ī 5430, also from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, carries the Prophet’s famous appraisal of the pair: “Have you not seen the verses that have been revealed to me tonight, the like of which has never been seen before? Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-falaq and Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-nās.” A parallel wording recorded elsewhere adds: “No one asks for refuge with the likes of them.” That is the authentic baseline for the surah’s rank among the ruqyah formulas of the Prophet ﷺ.

The target named in the surah is specific: al-Waswās al-Khannās — the Whisperer who retreats. The two names describe the same enemy from two angles. Waswās is the gerund-noun of a sound — the low, hissing suggestion that enters the chest below the threshold of articulate speech. Khannās is from the root kha-na-sa, meaning to retreat, withdraw, shrink back. Ibn Kathīr, citing Ibn ʿAbbās via Mujāhid, reports that when the servant remembers Allah, Shayṭān withdraws and shrinks; when the servant becomes heedless, Shayṭān returns and whispers again. The surah thus names the devil by his relationship to dhikr, not by his power — he is strong only in the space where Allah is forgotten. The final verse closes the definition: this whisperer operates from among the jinn and mankind — confirming the Qur’anic category (established also in Al-Anʿām 6:112) of a human Shayṭān, the person whose company plants the same whispers externally that the jinni Shayṭān plants internally. The surah’s wisdom is therefore double: seek refuge from the whisper of the unseen devil who comes when you forget your Lord, and from the whisper of the seen devil who gives you his hand when you abandon your prayer.

The historical occasion in which An-Nās and Al-Falaq were revealed together is the sorcery incident narrated in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5763, 3268 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2189: a Jewish man named Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam cast a spell on the Prophet ﷺ using a comb and hair in a well, and Allah informed him of it. The two surahs were revealed as the cure — one verse recited over each knot in the spell’s eleven knots, with each knot untying as the verses were read. This incident is mutawātir in meaning and the hadith is authentic in both Ṣaḥīḥs; it is why the two surahs are called al-Muʿawwidhatān. The theological point classical scholars draw from the incident — following al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, Ibn Taymiyyah, and Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī — is that the Prophet ﷺ remained protected from communicating any corrupted revelation (his ʿiṣmah in tablīgh was intact), but his human constitution could be affected like any other human body. Refuge in these two surahs is therefore not a weakness in the Prophet ﷺ; it is Allah’s teaching, through him, of the formula every believer needs.

The practical fiqh of the surah is simple and sunnah-rich. Recite An-Nās with Al-Falaq and Al-Ikhlāṣ three times after Fajr and Maghrib, and once after Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, and ʿIshā’ — the practice recorded in Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5082 and Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 3575 from ʿAbdullāh ibn Khubayb (ḥasan per al-Albānī in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Jāmiʿ). Recite the three Quls before sleep with the Bukhārī 5017 blowing-and-wiping method. Recite them when sick as ruqyah, as ʿĀ’ishah did for the Prophet ﷺ in his final illness (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5735, 5751). The surah’s power is not in a magic formula; it is in the relationship established by the three titles with which it opens — you ask the One who created you, owns you, and alone deserves your worship to protect you from the one who wants you to forget all three. That is the whole Qur’an in six verses, which is why Allah placed it at the end.
